title: Joy in practice
hookLine: piti and sukha: joy belongs on the path
tomorrow: who was the Buddha so glad for that he said it twice?

lines: A KING, NOW UNDER A TREE.
cards: There's a kind of guilt that shows up when something feels too good: a slow Sunday, a long laugh, as if joy must mean you're slacking. A group of monks once had that worry about a friend. Bhaddiya had been a king.

Now he was a monk who sat at the foot of trees in the forest, and again and again he said out loud: oh, what bliss! What bliss! The other monks were sure he was missing his palace and his old royal life.
So they went and told the Buddha.

teach.b: The Buddha called Bhaddiya and asked: is it true? It was. Why?
As king, Bhaddiya said, he had guards inside his rooms and outside, guards in the city and across the countryside, and still he lived afraid, on edge, trusting no one.

teach.h: UNDER A TREE, LIKE A WILD DEER.
teach.b: Now, alone at the root of a tree, he lived without fear, at ease, his mind, the text says, like a wild deer's. That was the bliss. The Buddha didn't scold him.
He answered with a short verse about a mind gone past fear and sorrow. Here's the teaching under the story. The suttas name two kinds of gladness on the path.

teach.h: PITI, THE LIFT. SUKHA, THE EASE.
teach.b: Sukha is a calmer ease, happiness at rest. Both arise in the early stages of deep meditation; in the first, the texts say, they are born of seclusion.
And piti is one of the seven factors of awakening, right beside mindfulness and energy.
So in Buddhist teaching joy isn't a prize for later, and it isn't a slip. It's part of the road. The story itself marks the difference: Bhaddiya's bliss wasn't the palace's pleasures coming back.
It was the gladness of having nothing left to guard.

how: In meditation teaching, piti (joy) and sukha (ease) are named among the qualities that arise as the mind settles; teachers encourage meditators to know them without clinging, as part of the path.

o: gladness that arises as part of the path itself
a prize you earn only after years of sitting
the pleasure of treating yourself after a sit

games.q: the king under the tree — tap the pairs.
p: once a king, now at the root of a tree
a calmer ease, happiness at rest

s: joy during meditation means you're doing it wrong
piti and sukha arise in the early stages of deep meditation, and piti is a factor of awakening.
Bhaddiya's 'what bliss' meant he missed his palace
the opposite: as king he lived afraid; alone under a tree, he lived free of fear.
the suttas list joy among the seven factors of awakening
piti sits beside mindfulness, energy and calm.

games.q: at a retreat, a friend felt lit up with joy during the sit, then panicked that she'd lost focus. what fits the Bhaddiya story?
o: joy from a settling mind is part of the path; know it without grabbing it.
joy means the mind slid back to pleasure; push it away and refocus.
chase that feeling every sit from now on; joy is the whole point.
games.why: the Buddha didn't scold Bhaddiya. the suttas name piti and sukha as part of deep meditation; the practice is to know them, not cling to them.

practice: If there's a cup of water or tea nearby, take one slow sip and follow it all the way: cool or warm, the taste, the swallow. If not, rest your attention in your hands and feel their warmth.
When any small gladness turns up during the sit, don't push it away and don't chase it; let it stay like a welcome guest.

wordCard.voice: Joy in practice: piti, the lift, and sukha, the ease. Part of the path, the suttas say, not a detour from it.

orig.note: Pali: joy, rapture, one of the seven factors of awakening.

carryVoice: Something to keep: joy belongs, like Bhaddiya's at the root of his tree, with nothing left to fear. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 2 (the first jhana: rapture and pleasure born of seclusion)
Samyutta Nikaya 46 (Bojjhanga Samyutta: the seven factors of awakening)
